articles.excerpt: Study games aren't just for the last day before break. Used well, they're some of the most effective review you can do. Here are eight that work for AP and SAT prep.

content.intro: Review games have a reputation as the thing teachers run when nobody wants to do real work. But a good study game is just retrieval practice with a scoreboard — and retrieval practice is one of the most effective ways to remember anything. Below are eight study games for AP exams and the SAT, grouped by whether you're playing alone, with friends or as a class, plus which subjects each one fits best.

sections.h2: With friends
sections.body:
### 1. Real-time quiz battles
Two players, same questions, points for accuracy and speed. It's the closest thing to a video game in studying, and it works for almost any subject. **Dogtor** has real-time quiz battles and ranked matchmaking for AP Biology, AP Psychology, AP Environmental Science, AP U.S. Government, SAT Reading and Writing and GRE vocabulary, with an explanation after every miss so losing still teaches you something.

### 2. Jeopardy-style review board
Make a board with one column per unit and point values by difficulty. Great the weekend before a unit test — and writing the questions is itself good review.

### 3. Teach-back tag
One person explains a concept for two minutes; the next has to add one thing or correct one thing. Especially good for AP Psych theories, APES cycles and AP Gov court cases. See also [All 15 Required Supreme Court Cases for AP Gov](/guide/ap-us-government-required-supreme-court-cases).

sections.h2: In class
sections.body:
### 4. Kahoot and Blooket
Fast, loud and great for vocabulary and recall. The limit: questions are usually short, so they're better for terms and facts than for the multi-step reasoning on real AP and SAT questions.

### 5. Quizlet Live
Teams race to match terms and definitions. Excellent for term-heavy units; pair it with exam-style practice afterwards.

sections.h2: Solo
sections.body:
### 6. Mistake-replay challenge
Every question you miss goes on a list. Each session starts by replaying five of them; a question only leaves the list when you get it right on two different days. It's the single most score-moving game on this page. Dogtor keeps this list for you automatically and uses it to pick what you should practice next.

### 7. SAT speed rounds
Set a timer for the real per-question pace and see how many you can answer accurately. Track your best score. This builds the pacing you'll need on test day — see [Digital SAT Reading and Writing question types](/guide/sat-reading-and-writing-question-types).

### 8. Notes-to-quiz
Turn your class notes into a quiz and play it until you hit 100%. Write the questions yourself, or upload notes or a PDF to Dogtor and let AI build a practice level from them.

sections.h2: How to make study games count
sections.body:
- **Mix in real exam formats** at least once a week — games are review, not a replacement for practice tests.
- **Play your weak units more than your strong ones.**
- **Keep it short and frequent.** Fifteen minutes a day of games beats a two-hour review party once a month.

For more ways to make prep enjoyable, read [How to Make Studying for AP Exams and the SAT Fun](/guide/how-to-make-studying-for-ap-and-sat-fun).

articles.title: How to Make Studying for AP Exams and the SAT Fun (9 Ideas That Still Raise Your Score)
articles.description: AP and SAT prep doesn't have to be miserable. Nine ways to make studying fun that are backed by how memory works: quiz games, battles with friends, streaks, tiny levels, teaching others and more — plus how to keep the fun from turning into procrastination.
tags: fun way to study for AP exams
articles.excerpt: The hardest part of AP and SAT prep isn't the content. It's opening the book. Here's how to make studying something you actually want to do — without trading away results.

content.intro: Most students don't fail AP exams or plateau on the SAT because the material is impossible. They fall behind because studying feels like a chore, so it gets pushed to tomorrow, then to the weekend, then to the week before the test. The fix isn't more willpower. It's making the work itself more enjoyable. The good news: the things that make studying fun — quizzing, competing, short wins, explaining to friends — are also some of the most effective ways to learn. Here are nine ideas that make prep fun **and** move your score.

sections.h2: Why fun study methods work (it's not just about mood)
sections.body: Two of the best-supported findings in learning science are the **testing effect** (retrieving an answer strengthens memory far more than rereading it) and **spaced practice** (short sessions spread over days beat one long cram). Games happen to be built on exactly those two things: you answer questions, you get instant feedback, and you come back tomorrow to keep a streak alive. So when studying feels like a game, you're usually not cutting corners — you're doing the high-value kind of practice more often.

sections.h2: 1. Turn review into a quiz battle with friends
sections.body: Competition is the fastest way to make 20 minutes of review fly by. Pick a unit, quiz each other, keep score. Apps make this effortless: in **Dogtor** you can add friends and battle them in real-time quizzes on AP Biology, AP Psychology, AP Environmental Science, AP U.S. Government, SAT Reading and Writing or GRE vocabulary — same questions, who's faster and more accurate. Losing a round still helps, because every miss comes with an explanation. More options in [Best Apps to Study With Friends](/guide/best-apps-to-study-with-friends).

sections.h2: 2. Shrink sessions into levels you can actually finish
sections.body: "Study AP Bio for two hours" is intimidating. "Clear one 10-question level on cell respiration" is not. Breaking prep into small, finishable chunks gives you a steady stream of small wins, which is what keeps games addictive. Aim for a few short levels a day instead of one marathon on Sunday.

sections.h2: 3. Keep a streak
sections.body: Streaks work because breaking one feels worse than doing ten minutes of practice. Track it on a calendar, in a habit app, or in a study app that counts it for you. The goal isn't long sessions; it's not missing days. Ten minutes every day beats two hours once a week for retention.

sections.h2: 4. Make your mistakes the main event
sections.body: Getting questions wrong is where the learning is — if you go back to them. Keep a mistake log (or let an app do it) and start each session by re-trying a few old misses. Treat it like replaying the boss level you lost. When you can get a question right in a different form a few days later, you've actually learned it, not just remembered the answer.

sections.h2: 5. Teach it to someone (or something)
sections.body: Explaining a concept out loud — to a friend, a younger sibling, or even your dog — exposes exactly where your understanding breaks. Take turns being "the teacher" in a study group, five minutes per topic. If you can't explain why an answer is right, that's your next thing to review.

sections.h2: 6. Play classroom-style review games at home
sections.body: Jeopardy-style boards, Kahoot or Blooket games your teacher shares, and Quizlet's live and match modes all turn content review into a game. They're great for vocabulary and fact-heavy units like AP Psych terms or the required Supreme Court cases in AP Gov. Pair them with real exam-style questions closer to test day.

sections.h2: 7. Turn your own notes into a quiz
sections.body: Rereading notes is passive and boring. Turning them into questions makes them active. You can write your own flashcards, or snap a photo of your notes or upload a PDF in Dogtor and let AI turn it into a practice level — handy for a class your teacher covers differently, or a subject not in any question bank yet.

sections.h2: 8. Get unstuck instantly
sections.body: Nothing kills momentum like a question you can't figure out and no one to ask until tomorrow. Use the answer explanation, a textbook, or an AI tutor to understand the step you're missing right away, then do one similar question to make sure it stuck. Keep the loop short: miss → understand → retry.

sections.h2: 9. Reward the process, not just the score
sections.body: Set small rewards for consistency: a week-long streak, a unit's mistake log cleared, a friend beaten in a rematch. Scores swing from practice test to practice test; habits are what actually move them.

sections.h2: How to keep "fun" from becoming procrastination
sections.body:
- **Always end on exam-style questions.** Games are great for review, but finish each week with questions in the real AP or SAT format and timing.
- **Let your weak spots pick the content.** Fun is easier when you only practice what you already know — resist that. Start from your mistakes.
- **Cap the setup time.** If you spend more time customizing a study app than studying, switch to something simpler.

If you want a full plan to put these habits into, see [How to Prepare for AP Exams](/guide/how-to-prepare-for-ap-exams) or [How to Prepare for the SAT](/guide/how-to-prepare-for-the-sat).

articles.title: AP Biology Exam Format, Explained: Sections, Timing, Unit Weights and FRQ Types
articles.description: How the AP Biology exam is structured: 60 multiple-choice questions and 6 free-response questions, how much each unit is worth, the six FRQ types, and what that means for how you study.
articles.excerpt: Two 90-minute sections, eight units with very different weights, and six predictable free-response question types. Here is the whole exam on one page.

content.intro: The AP Biology exam has **two sections of equal weight**: 60 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes, then 6 free-response questions in 90 minutes. Each section is **50% of your score**. Knowing exactly how those points are distributed tells you where your study hours pay off most.

sections.h2: The two sections at a glance
sections.body:
| Section | Questions | Time | Share of score |
|---|---|---|---|
| I: Multiple choice | 60 | 1 h 30 min | 50% |
| II: Free response | 6 (2 long, 4 short) | 1 h 30 min | 50% |

The exam is **hybrid digital**: you answer the multiple-choice questions and read the free-response questions in the College Board's Bluebook app, but you **handwrite** your free-response answers in a paper booklet. A four-function, scientific or graphing calculator is allowed in both sections, and you get an equations and formulas sheet.

That works out to about **90 seconds per multiple-choice question** and roughly **20 minutes per long free-response question** and 10 per short one.

Already took a practice test? Plug your results into the free [AP Biology score calculator](/ap-score-calculator/ap-biology) to estimate your AP score from 1 to 5.

sections.h2: How much each unit is worth
sections.body:
The Course and Exam Description gives a weight range for each unit on the multiple-choice section:

| Unit | Topic | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Chemistry of Life | 8–11% |
| 2 | Cell Structure and Function | 10–13% |
| 3 | Cellular Energetics | 12–16% |
| 4 | Cell Communication and Cell Cycle | 10–15% |
| 5 | Heredity | 8–11% |
| 6 | Gene Expression and Regulation | 12–16% |
| 7 | Natural Selection | 13–20% |
| 8 | Ecology | 10–15% |

Three units carry the most weight: **Natural Selection (up to 20%)**, **Cellular Energetics** and **Gene Expression and Regulation** (up to 16% each). Together they can be close to half the multiple-choice section. If you are short on time, make sure those three are solid before you polish Units 1 and 5.

sections.h2: The six free-response question types
sections.body:
The free-response section follows the same pattern every year, so you can practice each type on purpose:

1. **Interpreting and evaluating experimental results** (long): read an experiment, identify variables and controls, and justify conclusions.
2. **Interpreting and evaluating experimental results with graphing** (long): the same, plus building a correct graph from a data table.
3. **Scientific investigation** (short): design or critique an experiment.
4. **Conceptual analysis** (short): explain a biological process and predict what happens when it is disrupted.
5. **Analyze a model or visual representation** (short): interpret a diagram or model.
6. **Analyze data** (short): read a graph or table and draw a supported claim.

Notice that only one of the six is mainly about recalling content. The rest test **science practices**: designing experiments, graphing, reading data and arguing from evidence.

sections.h2: Skills the exam rewards
sections.body:
Every question is tied to one of six science practices: concept explanation, visual representations, questions and methods, representing and describing data, statistical tests and data analysis, and argumentation.

Two of those catch students out most often:

- **Graphing.** Label both axes with units, choose the right graph type (a line graph for continuous data, a bar graph for categories), and include error bars when the data give a standard error or confidence interval.
- **Statistics.** Be comfortable with the chi-square test: state the null hypothesis, compute degrees of freedom (number of categories minus one), and compare your value with the critical value on the formula sheet.

sections.h2: What this means for how you study
sections.body:
- **Weight your time by unit.** Spend the most time on Units 3, 6 and 7.
- **Practice the FRQ types, not just the content.** The College Board publishes past free-response questions with scoring guidelines on AP Central. Do them under time, then grade yourself strictly against the rubric.
- **Turn every miss into a pattern.** When you get a question wrong, note *why*: a content gap, a misread graph, or a weak justification. The fix is different for each.
- **Do short daily sets instead of rare long sessions.** Spacing your practice beats cramming for retention.

faq.question: How long is the AP Biology exam?
faq.answer: Three hours of testing time: 90 minutes for 60 multiple-choice questions and 90 minutes for 6 free-response questions.

faq.question: Can I use a calculator on the AP Biology exam?
faq.answer: Yes. A four-function, scientific or graphing calculator is allowed on both sections, and an equations and formulas sheet is provided.

faq.question: Which AP Biology units are the most important?
faq.answer: By weight, Unit 7 (Natural Selection, 13–20%), Unit 3 (Cellular Energetics, 12–16%) and Unit 6 (Gene Expression and Regulation, 12–16%).

articles.title: AP Biology Unit 3 Practice Questions: Cellular Energetics (with Explanations)
articles.description: Eight AP Biology Unit 3 practice questions on enzymes, cellular respiration, fermentation and photosynthesis, each with a full explanation of the right answer and the common traps.
articles.excerpt: Enzymes, respiration, fermentation and photosynthesis: eight exam-style questions with explanations for every answer, including why the wrong choices are tempting.

content.intro:
Unit 3, **Cellular Energetics**, is worth about **12–16%** of the AP Biology multiple-choice section and shows up in free-response questions about experiments too. These eight questions cover the ideas tested most often: enzyme activity, the electron transport chain, fermentation and photosynthesis.

Try each one before reading the answer. If you miss one, the explanation tells you which idea to review.

sections.h2: Enzymes (questions 1–2)
sections.body:
**1. An enzyme's activity is measured with and without a competitive inhibitor. As substrate concentration is increased to very high levels, what happens to the reaction rate in the presence of the inhibitor?**

- (A) It stays far below the uninhibited rate at every substrate concentration.
- (B) It approaches the same maximum rate as the uninhibited reaction.
- (C) It drops to zero because the inhibitor permanently changes the active site.
- (D) It exceeds the uninhibited rate because the inhibitor stabilizes the enzyme.

**Answer: B.** A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site. At very high substrate concentrations, substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor, so the reaction approaches the same maximum rate. Option C describes irreversible inhibition, not competitive inhibition.

**2. A human enzyme works best at 37 °C. When the temperature is raised to 60 °C, its activity drops sharply and does not recover after cooling. Which explanation is best supported?**

- (A) The high temperature broke the enzyme's peptide bonds, splitting it into amino acids.
- (B) The high temperature disrupted the bonds that hold the enzyme's tertiary structure, changing the shape of the active site.
- (C) The substrate molecules moved too fast to be converted into products.
- (D) The enzyme was used up by the reaction at high temperature.

**Answer: B.** Heat disrupts hydrogen bonds and other interactions that maintain tertiary structure. The protein denatures, the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits. Peptide bonds (A) are covalent and much more stable. Enzymes are not consumed by the reactions they catalyze (D).

sections.h2: Cellular respiration and fermentation (questions 3–5)
sections.body:
**3. During oxidative phosphorylation, where does ATP synthase make ATP, and which way do protons move through it?**

- (A) In the outer mitochondrial membrane; protons move from the matrix to the cytosol.
- (B) In the inner mitochondrial membrane; protons move from the intermembrane space into the matrix.
- (C) In the inner mitochondrial membrane; protons move from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
- (D) In the matrix; protons move from the cytosol into the matrix.

**Answer: B.** The electron transport chain pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building a gradient. ATP synthase, embedded in the inner membrane, lets protons flow back down that gradient into the matrix and uses the energy to make ATP. Option C describes the pumping, not ATP synthesis.

**4. Cyanide blocks the final protein complex of the electron transport chain, so electrons can no longer be passed to oxygen. What is the most likely immediate effect in the mitochondria?**

- (A) The proton gradient across the inner membrane increases.
- (B) Electron transport stops, the proton gradient is not maintained and ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation falls.
- (C) Glycolysis stops because it requires oxygen.
- (D) Oxygen consumption increases to compensate.

**Answer: B.** With the final electron acceptor step blocked, electrons back up and the chain stops pumping protons. Without a gradient, ATP synthase cannot make ATP. Glycolysis (C) does not require oxygen and can continue, which is why cells briefly rely on fermentation.

**5. Some cells ferment glucose to lactate when oxygen is scarce. What is the main benefit of fermentation for the cell?**

- (A) It produces more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
- (B) It regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep producing ATP.
- (C) It removes carbon dioxide from the cell.
- (D) It produces the oxygen needed for the electron transport chain.

**Answer: B.** Glycolysis reduces NAD⁺ to NADH. Without oxygen, NADH cannot be oxidized by the electron transport chain, so NAD⁺ runs out. Fermentation oxidizes NADH back to NAD⁺, letting glycolysis continue to make its 2 ATP per glucose. Fermentation yields far less ATP than aerobic respiration (A).

sections.h2: Photosynthesis (questions 6–7)
sections.body:
**6. In the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, where does the oxygen released by the plant come from?**

- (A) Carbon dioxide
- (B) Glucose
- (C) Water
- (D) RuBP

**Answer: C.** Photosystem II splits water to replace the electrons it loses when light excites its chlorophyll. That splitting releases O₂. The oxygen atoms in CO₂ end up in sugars, not in the oxygen gas released.

**7. Which statement correctly describes the Calvin cycle?**

- (A) It occurs in the thylakoid membrane and produces ATP and NADPH.
- (B) It occurs in the stroma and uses ATP and NADPH to turn fixed CO₂ into G3P.
- (C) It occurs only in the dark and does not depend on the light reactions.
- (D) It releases CO₂ as a by-product of breaking down glucose.

**Answer: B.** The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma. Rubisco fixes CO₂ to RuBP, then ATP and NADPH from the light reactions reduce the products to G3P, which the cell uses to build sugars. Although it doesn't use light directly, it depends on the ATP and NADPH the light reactions produce, so it stops soon after light is removed (C).

sections.h2: Putting it together (question 8)
sections.body:
**8. A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons. Electron transport and oxygen use continue, but ATP production drops sharply. Where does most of the energy released by electron transport go?**

- (A) It is stored as NADH.
- (B) It is released as heat.
- (C) It is used to pump more glucose into the cell.
- (D) It is stored in a larger proton gradient.

**Answer: B.** This is an uncoupler: electron transport still pumps protons, but they leak back across the membrane without passing through ATP synthase. The gradient can't be maintained (D), and the energy is lost as heat. Brown fat uses a protein that does this on purpose to generate body heat.

sections.h2: What to review if you missed some
sections.body:
- **Missed 1–2:** review how enzyme shape determines function, and the difference between competitive, noncompetitive and irreversible inhibition.
- **Missed 3, 4 or 8:** draw the inner mitochondrial membrane and follow electrons and protons step by step. Most mistakes come from mixing up which side the protons are pumped to.
- **Missed 5:** remember that fermentation exists to recycle NAD⁺, not to make extra ATP.
- **Missed 6–7:** list the inputs and outputs of the light reactions and the Calvin cycle side by side. Each stage's outputs are the other's inputs.

faq.question: How much of the AP Biology exam is Unit 3?
faq.answer: About 12–16% of the multiple-choice section, according to the College Board's Course and Exam Description. Unit 3 ideas also appear in free-response questions about experiments.

faq.question: What are the most tested topics in AP Biology Unit 3?
faq.answer: Enzyme structure and inhibition, how the electron transport chain builds a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase, the role of fermentation, and the inputs and outputs of the light reactions and the Calvin cycle.

articles.title: How to Self-Study AP Biology: A 16-Week Plan That Fits Around School
articles.description: A week-by-week plan to self-study AP Biology in about four months, weighted by how much each unit is worth, with practice-question and free-response routines that build exam skills.
tags: how to study for AP Biology
articles.excerpt: Sixteen weeks, about five hours a week. Spend longer on the heavy units, practice free-response questions from week three, and finish with timed practice exams.

content.intro: You can self-study AP Biology in about **four months at five hours a week** if you study by weight and practice the exam's skills from the start, not just at the end. This plan starts in January and leaves the last four weeks for review and full practice exams before the May exam.

sections.h2: Before you start: register for the exam
sections.body:
If your school doesn't offer AP Biology, you still need a school or test center to order the exam for you. **Exam ordering usually closes in the fall**, around mid-November, and later orders may carry an extra fee. Contact your school's AP coordinator, or search the College Board's AP course and exam finder for a test center that accepts outside students, as early as you can.

You'll also want:

- The free **AP Biology Course and Exam Description** from AP Central, so you know exactly what's in scope.
- **Past free-response questions with scoring guidelines**, also free on AP Central.
- One review book or video series you like. Don't collect five.

sections.h2: The 16-week plan
sections.body:
| Weeks | Focus | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Unit 1: Chemistry of Life | Lighter unit (8–11%); builds vocabulary you'll need |
| 2 | Unit 2: Cell Structure and Function | 10–13% |
| 3–4 | Unit 3: Cellular Energetics | 12–16%; respiration and photosynthesis take time |
| 5 | Unit 4: Cell Communication and Cell Cycle | 10–15% |
| 6 | Unit 5: Heredity | 8–11%; practice chi-square here |
| 7–8 | Unit 6: Gene Expression and Regulation | 12–16% |
| 9–10 | Unit 7: Natural Selection | 13–20%, the heaviest unit |
| 11–12 | Unit 8: Ecology | 10–15% |
| 13–14 | Weak-unit review | Driven by your mistake log |
| 15–16 | Full timed practice exams | Build stamina and pacing |

If you start later, compress the lighter units (1, 2 and 5) first and protect the time for Units 3, 6 and 7.

sections.h2: A weekly routine (about five hours)
sections.body:
- **Two learning sessions (60 minutes each):** read or watch the material for that week's unit and make a one-page summary from memory afterwards.
- **Four short practice sessions (20 minutes each):** multiple-choice questions on the current unit *plus* a few from earlier units. Mixing in old units is what keeps them from fading.
- **One free-response session (60 minutes):** from week 3, do one past free-response question under time, then grade it against the official scoring guideline.
- **Mistake review (20 minutes):** go through everything you got wrong that week and write down *why* — a gap in content, a misread graph or a weak justification.

sections.h2: Practicing free response the right way
sections.body:
The free-response section is half your score and follows six predictable question types. Most of the points come from **specific moves**: identifying the independent and dependent variables, naming a control, stating a prediction with a reason, and justifying a claim with data.

When you grade yourself, be strict: if the scoring guideline asks for a justification and you only gave a claim, you did not earn that point. After a few weeks you'll notice which moves you keep forgetting, and that list is your free-response checklist for test day.

sections.h2: The last month
sections.body:
- Take **one full timed practice exam per week** in weeks 15 and 16, in one sitting, with a calculator and the formula sheet.
- After each one, sort your mistakes by unit and by skill, and spend the following days only on the top two categories.
- In the final week, do short mixed sets daily and stop learning new material two days before the exam.

faq.question: Can you self-study AP Biology?
faq.answer: Yes. Many students self-study AP Biology. You need to arrange for a school or test center to order the exam for you, usually by mid-November, and plan around four months of steady study.

faq.question: How many hours does it take to self-study AP Biology?
faq.answer: Around 80 hours is a realistic target for most students: about five hours a week for 16 weeks. Students with a strong biology background may need less.

faq.question: What is the hardest unit in AP Biology?
faq.answer: It varies by student, but Units 3 (Cellular Energetics) and 6 (Gene Expression and Regulation) are often cited as the hardest, and Unit 7 (Natural Selection) carries the most weight.

articles.title: AP Psychology Exam Format, Explained: Units, Timing and the Two FRQ Types (AAQ and EBQ)
articles.description: How the redesigned AP Psychology exam works: 75 multiple-choice questions, two free-response questions (the Article Analysis Question and the Evidence-Based Question), five equally weighted units and how to study for each part.
articles.excerpt: Five units of equal weight, 75 multiple-choice questions and two very predictable free-response tasks. Here is the whole redesigned exam on one page.

content.intro: AP Psychology was redesigned for the 2024–25 school year. The course now has **five units of roughly equal weight**, and the free-response section has **two fixed question types**: the Article Analysis Question (AAQ) and the Evidence-Based Question (EBQ). Both reward the same skill: using psychological research as evidence, not just defining terms.

sections.h2: The two sections at a glance
sections.body:
| Section | Questions | Time | Share of score |
|---|---|---|---|
| I: Multiple choice | 75 | 1 h 30 min | about 67% |
| II: Free response | 2 (AAQ + EBQ) | 1 h 10 min | about 33% |

That is about **72 seconds per multiple-choice question**. Many multiple-choice questions come in sets built around a short scenario, a data table or a description of a study, so reading carefully matters as much as recall.

sections.h2: The five units
sections.body:
| Unit | Topic | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Biological Bases of Behavior | 15–25% |
| 2 | Cognition | 15–25% |
| 3 | Development and Learning | 15–25% |
| 4 | Social Psychology and Personality | 15–25% |
| 5 | Mental and Physical Health | 15–25% |

Because every unit has the same range, **there is no unit you can safely skip**. Research methods are no longer a separate unit; they are woven into every unit and tested directly in the free-response section.

sections.h2: FRQ 1: the Article Analysis Question (AAQ)
sections.body:
You get a summary of **one research study** and answer a set of short parts, usually worth **7 points** in total. Expect to:

- Identify the **research method** (experiment, correlational study, case study, and so on).
- Name the **independent and dependent variables**, or the variables being correlated, and give an **operational definition**.
- Describe the **sample** and whether the results can be **generalized** to a wider population.
- Interpret a **statistic** reported in the study (a mean, a correlation coefficient, a p-value).
- State an **ethical guideline** the researchers followed.
- Explain whether the findings **support a hypothesis**, using data from the article.

The AAQ is the most coachable part of the exam: the parts come from a short list, so practicing the research-methods vocabulary pays off directly.

sections.h2: FRQ 2: the Evidence-Based Question (EBQ)
sections.body:
You get **three short source summaries** about one topic and must build an argument, also worth about **7 points**. Typically you:

1. **Propose a claim** that answers the prompt.
2. **Support it with evidence from two of the sources**, citing them specifically.
3. **Explain how each piece of evidence supports your claim** using a relevant psychological concept.

The most common way to lose points is to quote a source without explaining *why* it supports the claim. Every piece of evidence needs a "because" sentence that links it to a named psychological concept.

sections.h2: How to study for the redesigned exam
sections.body:
- **Learn concepts with examples, not definitions alone.** Multiple-choice questions describe a scenario and ask which concept it shows. For each term, know one concrete example.
- **Master research methods early.** They appear in every unit and in both FRQs: variables, operational definitions, random sampling versus random assignment, correlation versus causation, and ethics.
- **Write one AAQ and one EBQ a week** from the released samples on AP Central, then grade yourself against the scoring guidelines.
- **Mix units in your practice.** Because all five units carry similar weight, short mixed review sessions protect you from forgetting the units you studied first.

articles.title: AP Environmental Science (APES) Exam Format: Unit Weights, FRQ Types and the Math You Need
articles.description: How the AP Environmental Science exam is structured: 80 multiple-choice questions and 3 free-response questions, the weight of each of the nine units, and the calculation skills APES expects.
articles.excerpt: Eighty multiple-choice questions, three free-response questions and nine units — with Global Change worth the most. Plus the handful of calculations that show up every year.

content.intro: The AP Environmental Science exam has **80 multiple-choice questions** worth 60% of your score and **3 free-response questions** worth 40%. It covers nine units, but they are not equal: **Unit 9, Global Change, carries the most weight**, and one free-response question always involves calculations.

sections.h2: The two sections at a glance
sections.body:
| Section | Questions | Time | Share of score |
|---|---|---|---|
| I: Multiple choice | 80 | 1 h 30 min | 60% |
| II: Free response | 3 | 1 h 10 min | 40% |

That is roughly **67 seconds per multiple-choice question** and about **23 minutes per free-response question**. Multiple-choice questions often come in sets that share a graph, table, map or short text, so practice reading data quickly.

Already took a practice test? Plug your results into the free [APES score calculator](/ap-score-calculator/apes) to estimate your AP score from 1 to 5.

sections.h2: How much each unit is worth
sections.body:
| Unit | Topic | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The Living World: Ecosystems | 6–8% |
| 2 | The Living World: Biodiversity | 6–8% |
| 3 | Populations | 10–15% |
| 4 | Earth Systems and Resources | 10–15% |
| 5 | Land and Water Use | 10–15% |
| 6 | Energy Resources and Consumption | 10–15% |
| 7 | Atmospheric Pollution | 7–10% |
| 8 | Aquatic and Terrestrial Pollution | 7–10% |
| 9 | Global Change | 15–20% |

Unit 9 (climate change, ozone depletion, ocean acidification, invasive species) is the single biggest unit. Units 3 to 6 together are also a large share of the exam, so do not leave them until the end.

sections.h2: The three free-response question types
sections.body:
1. **Design an investigation.** You read a scenario or study, identify a research question, the independent and dependent variables and a control, and explain the results.
2. **Analyze an environmental problem and propose a solution.** You describe an environmental issue, explain its causes and effects, and propose and justify a solution.
3. **Analyze an environmental problem and propose a solution doing calculations.** The same task, plus calculations. You must **show your work and include units** to earn full credit.

In every type, "describe" and "explain" are different tasks. "Describe" asks for what happens; "explain" asks *why* or *how*. Answering a describe-level sentence to an explain prompt is a common way to lose points.

sections.h2: The math APES actually uses
sections.body:
The calculations are simple, but they punish careless setup. The same handful appear again and again:

- **Percent change:** (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
- **Rule of 70:** doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate (in percent).
- **Unit conversions and dimensional analysis:** for example kWh per day to kWh per year, or gallons to liters.
- **Scientific notation:** multiplying and dividing very large numbers such as energy use or population.
- **Energy and efficiency:** output energy ÷ input energy, and the 10% rule for energy passed between trophic levels.
- **Half-life:** how much of a substance remains after a number of half-lives.

Write every step with units. Graders give credit for a correct setup even when the final arithmetic slips.

sections.h2: How to study for APES
sections.body:
- **Spend extra time on Unit 9** and on the middle units (3–6), which make up most of the exam.
- **Learn each environmental problem as a chain:** cause → effect on the environment → effect on humans → solution. Free-response questions follow exactly that chain.
- **Do one calculation problem a day** so the setup becomes automatic.
- **Practice with released FRQs** from AP Central and grade yourself against the scoring guidelines, paying attention to which verbs (identify, describe, explain, justify) earn which points.

articles.title: All 15 Required Supreme Court Cases for AP U.S. Government, Explained in Plain English
articles.description: A one-page guide to the 15 required Supreme Court cases in AP U.S. Government and Politics: what each case decided, the constitutional clause behind it, and how the cases show up in the SCOTUS comparison FRQ.
articles.excerpt: Fifteen cases, one table each for what was decided and why it matters — plus how to use them in the SCOTUS comparison free-response question.

content.intro: AP U.S. Government and Politics requires you to know **15 Supreme Court cases** (and 9 foundational documents). They appear in multiple-choice questions and in one of the four free-response questions, the **SCOTUS comparison**, where you compare a required case to a case you have never seen. For each case, know three things: **the facts in one sentence, the decision, and the constitutional clause** it turned on.

sections.h2: Federalism and the powers of government
sections.body:
| Case | Year | What the Court decided | Clause or principle |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Marbury v. Madison** | 1803 | Established **judicial review**: courts can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution. | Article III |
| **McCulloch v. Maryland** | 1819 | Congress could create a national bank, and a state could not tax it. | Necessary and Proper Clause; Supremacy Clause |
| **United States v. Lopez** | 1995 | Struck down a federal ban on guns near schools because it went **beyond the Commerce Clause**. | Commerce Clause; limits on federal power |

McCulloch expanded federal power; Lopez is the classic example of the Court limiting it. Expect questions that pair the two.

Already took a practice test? Plug your results into the free [AP U.S. Government score calculator](/ap-score-calculator/ap-us-government) to estimate your AP score from 1 to 5.

sections.h2: First Amendment: religion
sections.body:
| Case | Year | What the Court decided | Clause |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Engel v. Vitale** | 1962 | Official, school-sponsored prayer in public schools violates the Constitution, even if voluntary. | Establishment Clause |
| **Wisconsin v. Yoder** | 1972 | Amish parents could not be forced to send children to school past eighth grade. | Free Exercise Clause |

A quick way to keep them apart: Engel stops the government from **establishing** religion; Yoder protects an individual's **free exercise** of it.

sections.h2: First Amendment: speech and press
sections.body:
| Case | Year | What the Court decided | Principle |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tinker v. Des Moines** | 1969 | Students could wear black armbands to protest the Vietnam War; symbolic speech at school is protected unless it substantially disrupts learning. | Symbolic speech |
| **Schenck v. United States** | 1919 | Upheld a conviction for distributing anti-draft leaflets in wartime; speech creating a **"clear and present danger"** can be limited. | Limits on speech |
| **New York Times Co. v. United States** | 1971 | The government could not block publication of the Pentagon Papers; **prior restraint** carries a heavy presumption against it. | Freedom of the press |
| **Citizens United v. FEC** | 2010 | Limits on independent political spending by corporations and unions violate free speech. | Political speech; campaign finance |

sections.h2: Rights of the accused, privacy and incorporation
sections.body:
| Case | Year | What the Court decided | Clause |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gideon v. Wainwright** | 1963 | States must provide a lawyer to defendants in felony cases who cannot afford one. | Sixth Amendment, incorporated through the Fourteenth |
| **Roe v. Wade** | 1973 | Recognized a right to privacy covering a woman's decision to have an abortion. | Due Process Clause (Fourteenth Amendment) |
| **McDonald v. Chicago** | 2010 | The Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms applies to the states. | Selective incorporation |

Note: Roe v. Wade was **overturned in 2022** by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization. Check the current Course and Exam Description on AP Central for how the College Board treats Roe and Dobbs this year.

sections.h2: Civil rights, representation and elections
sections.body:
| Case | Year | What the Court decided | Clause |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Brown v. Board of Education** | 1954 | Racially segregated public schools are unconstitutional; "separate but equal" has no place in public education. | Equal Protection Clause |
| **Baker v. Carr** | 1962 | Courts can hear challenges to how legislative districts are drawn, which led to **"one person, one vote."** | Equal Protection Clause |
| **Shaw v. Reno** | 1993 | Districts drawn based mainly on race must meet strict scrutiny (racial gerrymandering). | Equal Protection Clause |

sections.h2: How to use the cases in the SCOTUS comparison FRQ
sections.body:
The SCOTUS comparison question describes a case you have not studied and asks you to:

1. **Identify a similarity or difference** between it and a required case.
2. **Explain how the facts or reasoning** of the required case relate to the new one.
3. **Describe an action** that people or institutions could take in response to the decision (for example, passing a law, filing new lawsuits or proposing an amendment).

The skill is matching the **constitutional clause**. If the new case involves a student protest, reach for Tinker; school prayer, Engel; districting, Baker or Shaw; a federal law based on commerce, Lopez. That is why the clause column in the tables above matters more than the dates.

faq.question: How many Supreme Court cases do you need to know for AP Gov?
faq.answer: Fifteen required cases, listed in the College Board's Course and Exam Description, along with nine foundational documents.

faq.question: Do I need to memorize the years of AP Gov court cases?
faq.answer: Years help with context, but the exam rewards knowing what each case decided and which constitutional clause it involved, so you can compare it with an unfamiliar case.

faq.question: What is the SCOTUS comparison FRQ?
faq.answer: One of the four AP U.S. Government free-response questions. It describes a non-required Supreme Court case and asks you to compare it with one of the 15 required cases.

articles.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing: Every Question Type and How to Approach It
articles.description: A guide to the digital SAT Reading and Writing section: its two adaptive modules, the four content domains, each question type from Words in Context to Rhetorical Synthesis, and a strategy for each.
articles.excerpt: Fifty-four short questions in two adaptive modules, four domains and about ten recurring question types. Learn the types and the section becomes predictable.

content.intro: The digital SAT's Reading and Writing section has **54 questions in two modules of 27**, with **32 minutes per module**. Every question has its own short passage, so instead of long reading passages you face a fast series of small tasks. The good news: those tasks come from a short list of **recurring question types**, and each has a reliable approach.

sections.h2: How the section works
sections.body:
| Part | Questions | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Module 1 | 27 | 32 min |
| Module 2 | 27 | 32 min |
| **Total** | **54** | **64 min** |

The section is **adaptive by module**: how well you do in Module 1 decides whether Module 2 is easier or harder. A strong Module 1 is the route to a top score, so accuracy early on matters. That works out to about **71 seconds per question**, and questions are grouped by type, roughly in the order of the domains below.

sections.h2: Domain 1: Craft and Structure (about 28%)
sections.body:
- **Words in Context:** choose the word that best fits a blank, or the meaning of a word as used in the text. *Approach:* predict your own word from the clues in the passage before you look at the choices.
- **Text Structure and Purpose:** identify the main purpose of a text or the function of one sentence. *Approach:* ask "why did the author write this?" and match the verb in the answer (argues, describes, challenges) to what the text actually does.
- **Cross-Text Connections:** two short texts; how would the author of Text 2 respond to Text 1? *Approach:* summarize each author's position in a few words first, then compare.

sections.h2: Domain 2: Information and Ideas (about 26%)
sections.body:
- **Central Ideas and Details:** what the text mainly says, or what it states about a detail. *Approach:* the right answer is usually a paraphrase; reject choices that are true in real life but not stated.
- **Command of Evidence (textual):** which quotation or finding would best support or weaken a claim. *Approach:* restate the claim precisely, then test each choice against it.
- **Command of Evidence (quantitative):** use data from a table or graph to complete a statement. *Approach:* check that the answer matches both the data **and** the claim in the passage; many wrong answers are accurate about the graph but irrelevant to the claim.
- **Inferences:** choose the most logical completion of a text. *Approach:* the answer must follow directly from the passage, not from outside knowledge.

sections.h2: Domain 3: Standard English Conventions (about 26%)
sections.body:
- **Boundaries:** punctuation between clauses and phrases — periods, semicolons, colons, commas and dashes. *Approach:* decide whether each side is an independent clause; a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.
- **Form, Structure and Sense:** subject–verb agreement, verb tense, pronoun agreement, possessives and modifiers. *Approach:* find the true subject by crossing out phrases between it and the verb.

This domain has the most learnable rules on the whole test. A few weeks of focused practice usually moves this score more than any other.

sections.h2: Domain 4: Expression of Ideas (about 20%)
sections.body:
- **Transitions:** choose the word or phrase that links two sentences logically (however, therefore, for example, similarly). *Approach:* decide the relationship first — contrast, cause and effect, example or continuation — then pick the transition.
- **Rhetorical Synthesis:** a student's bulleted notes and a goal ("emphasize a difference", "introduce the study to a new audience"). *Approach:* ignore which answer sounds best; pick the only one that **accomplishes the stated goal** using the notes.

sections.h2: A study plan that works
sections.body:
- **Take a full practice test in the Bluebook app** to learn your weakest question types.
- **Drill one question type at a time**, then mix them. Short daily sets of 10–15 questions beat one long weekend session.
- **Log every miss by type and reason**: vocabulary, misread claim, grammar rule, or time pressure. Your log tells you what to practice next.
- **Learn the grammar rules explicitly.** Boundaries and agreement questions are the fastest points to gain.

faq.answer: Yes. It adapts by module: your performance in Module 1 determines whether you get an easier or harder Module 2.

faq.answer: For most students, the Standard English Conventions questions (punctuation and grammar) and Transitions questions, because they follow learnable rules.

articles.title: How to Study GRE Vocabulary: A Method That Sticks (Not Just a Word List)
articles.description: How much vocabulary the GRE Verbal section really tests, how Text Completion and Sentence Equivalence use vocabulary, and a spaced-practice method for learning GRE words so you remember them on test day.
articles.excerpt: A few hundred high-frequency words, learned in context and reviewed on a schedule, beat a 3,000-word list you cram once.

content.intro: Vocabulary matters on the GRE, but **memorizing a giant word list is the least efficient way to learn it**. Two of the three Verbal question types — Text Completion and Sentence Equivalence — depend heavily on word knowledge, and the words that show up are a fairly stable set of high-frequency academic words. Learn those in context, review them on a schedule, and practice them inside real question formats.

sections.h2: Where vocabulary shows up on the GRE
sections.body:
| Question type | What it asks | How much vocabulary matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Text Completion** | Fill one to three blanks in a short passage | High |
| **Sentence Equivalence** | Pick the **two** words that each complete a sentence with the same meaning | Very high |
| **Reading Comprehension** | Answer questions about passages | Moderate (dense academic prose) |

Since 2023 the GRE General Test is shorter, with two Verbal sections. The Verbal question types themselves did not change, so vocabulary still drives a large share of the Verbal score.

sections.h2: Step 1: Pick the right words
sections.body:
Start with a list of roughly **300–500 high-frequency GRE words** rather than several thousand. Good GRE words share a profile: academic, often about attitude or argument, and easy to confuse with each other.

Group them by meaning instead of alphabetically. For example:

- **Praise:** laud, extol, commend, acclaim
- **Criticize:** censure, disparage, deride, castigate
- **Hard to pin down:** equivocal, ambiguous, enigmatic, inscrutable
- **Stubborn:** obdurate, intransigent, recalcitrant, obstinate

Groups mirror how Sentence Equivalence works: the two right answers are near-synonyms, so knowing a word's group is often enough.

sections.h2: Step 2: Learn each word in context
sections.body:
For each new word, write down:

1. A **short definition in your own words**.
2. **One sentence** that uses it the way the GRE would (academic, about an argument or a person's attitude).
3. **Its tone**: positive, negative or neutral.

Tone alone answers many questions. In a Text Completion, if the passage signals that a critic disliked a book, you can eliminate every positive word even before you know all the definitions.

sections.h2: Step 3: Review on a spaced schedule
sections.body:
You forget most new words within days unless you see them again. Review each word **one day, three days, a week and two weeks** after you first learn it. Words you miss go back to the start of the cycle.

Keep sessions short: **15–20 minutes a day** of mixed review is far more effective than two hours on a Sunday. Ten new words a day for six weeks covers about 400 words with plenty of review time.

sections.h2: Step 4: Practice inside real question formats
sections.body:
Recognizing a word on a flashcard is not the same as using it under time pressure. Once a week, do timed sets of Text Completion and Sentence Equivalence questions:

- **Read the sentence and predict your own word** before looking at the choices.
- Look for **signal words**: *although*, *however* and *despite* flip the meaning; *because*, *thus* and *indeed* continue it.
- In Sentence Equivalence, **find the pair first**. Two choices that mean the same thing and fit the sentence are almost always the answer.

Add every word you miss to your review list. Your mistakes are your best word list.

faq.question: How many vocabulary words do I need for the GRE?
faq.answer: Most students do well by mastering 300–500 high-frequency words and learning to use context and tone, rather than memorizing thousands of words.

faq.question: Which GRE questions test vocabulary?
faq.answer: Text Completion and Sentence Equivalence depend most on vocabulary. Reading Comprehension also uses dense academic language.

faq.question: How long does it take to learn GRE vocabulary?
faq.answer: With about 15–20 minutes a day of new words plus spaced review, around six weeks is enough to learn roughly 400 words well.

articles.title: AP Exam 30-Day Study Plan: A Week-by-Week Countdown for Any AP Subject
articles.description: A 30-day AP exam study plan you can apply to any subject: find your weak units, fix them in weeks one and two, practice free-response and timed sections in week three, and review your mistakes in the final week.
tags: how to study for AP exams
articles.excerpt: One month is enough to move an AP score if you spend it on your weakest units, not on rereading everything. Here's the plan, week by week.

content.intro: AP exams are given over two weeks in May, and the final month before your exam is when scores can still move the most. It's also when it's easiest to panic and reread everything. The fix is a plan: **find your weakest units, spend most of your time there, practice the exam format, then review your mistakes**. This 30-day plan works for any AP subject.

sections.h2: Before day 1: find your weak units
sections.body:
Spend one session on a **weakness check**. Take a released practice exam or your AP Classroom progress checks, and list the units and question types where you lose the most points. Then compare that list with the unit weights in your course's Course and Exam Description.

The rule for the month: **spend your time where weak meets heavy.** A weak unit worth 20% of the exam deserves far more time than a weak unit worth 6%. (Subject guides: [AP Biology](/guide/ap-biology-exam-format), [AP Psychology](/guide/ap-psychology-exam-format), [AP Environmental Science](/guide/ap-environmental-science-exam-format).)

sections.h2: Weeks 1–2: fix your weak units
sections.body:
Each day, pick **one or two weak units**. For each one:

1. **20 minutes:** review the key concepts (class notes, a Khan Academy or AP Daily video).
2. **40 minutes:** practice questions on just that unit.
3. **10 minutes:** check every miss and write down *why* you missed it.

Use a **70 / 20 / 10 split**: 70% of your time on weak units, 20% keeping strong units fresh, 10% as buffer. The goal of these two weeks isn't to cover everything. It's to cut down the number of units where you reliably lose points.

sections.h2: Week 3: practice the format under time
sections.body:
Switch from learning to performing.

- **Every other day**, do one **timed section**: the full multiple-choice section, or a set of free-response questions.
- **Grade free-response answers** against the official scoring guidelines on AP Central. Be strict; points come from specific wording.
- **Add every wrong or unsure question to your mistake list.**

Pacing is a skill. Students who know the content often lose points simply by running out of time on the last questions.

sections.h2: Week 4: mistake review and rest
sections.body:
In the final week, **stop starting new material**. Two jobs:

1. **Work through your mistake list from start to finish.** Every question you got wrong this month should now be one you get right.
2. **Get your body on exam time.** AP exams start in the morning or early afternoon, so shift your sleep and do your review at that time of day.

The day before the exam, review lightly and go to bed early. A good night's sleep is worth more than two extra hours of cramming.

sections.h2: Making the plan stick
sections.body:
The plan only works if you keep showing up for 30 days. Three things help:

- **Keep your practice in one place.** Switching between PDFs, notebooks and websites wastes energy. In Dogtor, practice, explanations and your mistake book live in one app, so the weak-unit drill and the final-week review take one tap.
- **Make it social.** Battle a friend on the units you're both reviewing; a little competition makes week three much less of a grind.
- **Track it visibly.** Print the plan, stick it on your desk and check off each day.

To see where a practice test puts you, try the free [AP score calculators](/ap-score-calculator) for APES, AP Biology, AP Psychology and AP U.S. Government.

faq.question: Is one month enough to study for an AP exam?
faq.answer: One month is enough to raise your score meaningfully if you've taken the course, as long as you focus on your weakest high-weight units, practice timed sections and review your mistakes.

faq.question: How many hours a day should I study for an AP exam?
faq.answer: For one exam, about an hour a day for 30 days is a solid plan. If you're taking several exams, rotate subjects and prioritize the earliest exam dates.

faq.question: What should I do the week before an AP exam?
faq.answer: Stop learning new material, review every question you got wrong during your prep, and adjust your sleep so you're alert at the exam's start time.

content.intro: A month is enough time to raise your digital SAT score if you **study by question type** instead of rereading everything. The digital SAT is short and predictable: two sections, each with two adaptive modules, and a fixed set of question types. Here's a four-week plan at about **an hour a day**.

sections.h2: The test in one table
sections.body:
| Section | Modules | Questions | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading and Writing | 2 | 54 | 64 min |
| Math | 2 | 44 | 70 min |

Both sections are **adaptive by module**: your first module decides whether the second is easier or harder, so accuracy early on matters. The Math section has a built-in Desmos graphing calculator, and you can also bring an approved calculator. Scores range from 400 to 1600.

sections.h2: Day 1: take a full practice test in Bluebook
sections.body:
Download the College Board's **Bluebook** app and take a full-length practice test under real timing. Then list your misses by **question type** (for example Transitions, Boundaries, Inferences, linear equations, percentages). Your three or four weakest types become your focus for the next two weeks.

For a breakdown of every Reading and Writing question type, see [Digital SAT Reading and Writing question types](/guide/sat-reading-and-writing-question-types).

sections.h2: Weeks 1–2: drill your weakest question types
sections.body:
Each day, about an hour:

- **30 minutes:** one weak question type. Learn the rule or method, then do 10–15 questions of just that type.
- **20 minutes:** mixed practice across both sections to keep everything else fresh.
- **10 minutes:** review every miss and write the reason: rule I didn't know, misread the question, careless math or time pressure.

The fastest gains are usually in **Standard English Conventions** (punctuation and grammar), **Transitions** and **Math basics** such as linear equations and percentages, because they follow learnable rules.

sections.h2: Week 3: practice full modules under time
sections.body:
- Take a **second full Bluebook practice test** at the start of the week and compare your question-type results with day 1.
- On the other days, do **one timed module** a day, alternating Reading and Writing and Math.
- Practice **pacing**: in Reading and Writing that's a little over a minute per question; flag hard questions, move on and come back.

sections.h2: Week 4: mistake review and test-day prep
sections.body:
- **Redo every question you missed** this month until you get each one right and can explain why.
- Take **one last practice test** early in the week, not the day before.
- **Get test-day logistics ready:** update Bluebook, charge your device, check your admission ticket and the test center's rules.
- **Sleep.** The night before, review lightly and go to bed on time.

sections.h2: Keep going for all four weeks
sections.body:
An hour a day is easy to plan and hard to keep up. Short daily sessions beat weekend marathons, and having a friend preparing at the same time helps a lot.

Dogtor's SAT Reading and Writing island fits the daily drill: bite-sized levels, instant explanations for every miss, a mistake book for week four and quiz battles you can play with a friend who's taking the same test date.

tags: how to prepare for the SAT
articles.excerpt: The gap isn't made in the last month — it's made by how you use the years and months before. Here's what to do in each grade, with any amount of time left, at any score level.

content.intro: "When should I start studying for the SAT?" There's no single right answer, but there is a right **order**. Freshman year builds the skills the test measures, sophomore and junior years turn them into test-taking skills, and the final months are about choosing what to fix. This guide lays out what to do in each grade, how to plan backward from your test date and how strategy changes depending on the score you're aiming for.

sections.h2: What to do in each grade
sections.body:
| Grade | Goal | What to do | What can wait |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9th | **Build the base** | Read widely, take algebra seriously, build a daily homework habit | SAT practice tests |
| 10th | **Get familiar** | Take the PSAT 10 or PSAT/NMSQT if your school offers it; review the results by question type | Expensive prep courses |
| 11th | **Prepare and test** | Take the PSAT/NMSQT in the fall, a Bluebook practice test, then a focused prep plan before your first SAT | Cramming every topic at once |
| 12th | **Retake if needed** | One more targeted round of prep, often for a fall test date | Starting from scratch |

Most students take their first SAT in the spring of junior year and, if needed, retake it in the summer or fall of senior year. Starting serious prep **two to three months before your first test date** is plenty when the foundation is there.

sections.h2: Plan backward from your test date
sections.body:
| Time left | Goal | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 6 months | **Fix foundations** | Diagnose with a Bluebook test, relearn weak math topics and grammar rules, build a daily practice habit |
| 3 months | **Raise the score** | Drill your weakest question types, one timed module a few times a week, a practice test every 3–4 weeks |
| 1 month | **Lock it in** | Timed full tests, mistake review, test-day logistics |

Six months is about building; three months is the main score-raising window; the final month is about consistency, not new material. For a day-by-day version of the last stretch, see the [SAT One-Month Study Plan](/guide/sat-one-month-study-plan).

sections.h2: Different score goals need different strategies
sections.body:
**Aiming for 1400+: protect your accuracy.**
- At this level, a few careless mistakes cost you the most. Sort every miss into "didn't know" and "slipped", and build a check habit for the slips.
- Make Module 1 count. Both sections adapt by module, so a strong first module unlocks the harder second module and the highest scores.
- Practice the hardest question types (Rhetorical Synthesis, Inferences, nonlinear functions) under time.

**Stuck around 1100–1300: master the most common question types.**
- This is the range where students gain the most points fastest.
- Learn the grammar rules for Boundaries and Form, Structure and Sense, and nail linear equations, percentages and ratios in Math.
- Keep a mistake log and redo every miss a week later.

**Below 1000: collect the points within reach.**
- Don't try to fix everything. Pick the two or three question types you're closest to getting right.
- Use the Desmos calculator built into Bluebook for graphing and checking answers.
- Do a short set every day; seeing progress keeps you going.

sections.h2: How to study each section
sections.body:
| Section | What it tests | How to practice |
|---|---|---|
| Reading and Writing (54 questions, 64 min) | Vocabulary in context, reading for evidence, grammar, transitions | Drill by question type; learn grammar rules explicitly; predict an answer before reading the choices |
| Math (44 questions, 70 min) | Algebra, advanced math, problem-solving and data analysis, geometry and trigonometry | Practice by topic; learn the Desmos shortcuts; write out the setup for word problems |

The common thread: **know the question types first, then choose the practice method**. For a full list of Reading and Writing question types and strategies, see [Digital SAT Reading and Writing question types](/guide/sat-reading-and-writing-question-types).

sections.h2: Why hard work sometimes doesn't move your score
sections.body:
1. **All input, no output.** Watching videos and rereading notes feels productive, but only practice questions show you what you can actually do.
2. **Reviewing answers instead of mistakes.** Checking the right answer isn't enough; write down *why* you missed it.
3. **Avoiding practice tests.** The sooner you see your gaps, the more time you have to close them.
4. **Switching resources every week.** Stick with one plan for at least three weeks before judging it.
5. **Ignoring pacing.** Many students know the content but run out of time; practice timed modules.
6. **Adding new material in the final weeks.** Late in your prep, reviewing your mistakes beats starting a new book.

sections.h2: Make the plan easy to stick with
sections.body: Any plan only works if you show up most days. Dogtor's SAT Reading and Writing island is built for that: short practice levels with a cute corgi study buddy, streaks that make a daily habit easy, quiz battles with friends taking the same test date, and a mistake book that brings back every question you got wrong. Pair it with official Bluebook practice tests and you've covered both the daily habit and the real test format. For more tools, see [Best AP and SAT Prep Apps](/guide/best-ap-and-sat-prep-apps).

faq.question: When should I start studying for the SAT?
faq.answer: Build reading and algebra skills in 9th and 10th grade, then start focused SAT prep two to three months before your first test date, usually in junior year.

faq.question: Is 3 months enough to prepare for the SAT?
faq.answer: Yes, for most students. Three months of regular practice organized by question type, with a practice test every few weeks and mistake review, is enough to raise a score meaningfully.

faq.question: How many hours a day should I study for the SAT?
faq.answer: About 30–60 minutes on most days is a solid pace, plus a longer timed session or practice test on weekends. Consistency matters more than total hours.

faq.question: Should I take the PSAT?
faq.answer: If your school offers it, yes. The PSAT is good practice with the same question types, and in junior year the PSAT/NMSQT is also the qualifying test for the National Merit Scholarship Program.

faq.question: How many times should I take the SAT?
faq.answer: Many students take it twice, once in junior year and once in the summer or fall of senior year. Check how your target colleges treat multiple scores, since policies such as superscoring vary.

articles.title: How to Prepare for AP Exams: A Full-Year Plan, Strategies by Score Goal and Subject Tips
articles.description: How to prepare for AP exams from September to May: what to do each part of the school year, how to plan backward from exam day, strategies for aiming at a 5, a 4 or a passing 3, subject tips for AP Biology, Psychology, Environmental Science and U.S. Government, and the mistakes to avoid.
tags: how to prepare for AP exams
how to get a 5 on AP
articles.excerpt: AP scores are decided long before May. Here's what to do from the first week of class to exam day, how to adjust for the score you want, and what each subject rewards.

content.intro: AP exams are given in May, but the students who do best don't start in April. They keep up during the year, start review early enough to fix weak units and practice the exam format before test day. This guide covers what to do in each part of the school year, how to plan backward from your exam date, how strategy changes depending on whether you're aiming for a 5 or a solid 3, and what each subject rewards.

sections.h2: What to do across the school year
sections.body:
| When | Goal | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| September–November | **Keep up** | Understand each unit as it's taught, fix test mistakes right away, make sure you're registered for the exam (schools usually order exams by mid-November) |
| December–February | **Connect units** | Start a mistake log, do the AP Classroom progress checks, try a few released free-response questions |
| March–April | **Start review** | Find your weak units, revisit early units you've forgotten, practice timed sections |
| May | **Perform** | Full practice exams, mistake review, rest |

The biggest trap is treating early units as "done". By May you've forgotten much of what you learned in September, so short mixed reviews throughout the year save a lot of time later.

sections.h2: Plan backward from exam day
sections.body:
| Time left | Goal | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| 3 months | **Fill the gaps** | Weakness check with a released exam; relearn weak, high-weight units |
| 6 weeks | **Practice the format** | Timed multiple-choice sections, free-response questions graded against the official scoring guidelines |
| 2 weeks | **Lock it in** | Mistake review, one full practice exam, adjust your sleep to the exam time |

For a detailed final-month schedule, see the [AP Exam 30-Day Study Plan](/guide/ap-exam-30-day-study-plan).

sections.h2: Strategy depends on your score goal
sections.body:
AP exams are scored 1 to 5. Many colleges award credit or placement for a 3 or higher, while selective colleges often look for a 4 or 5; check each college's AP credit policy.

**Aiming for a 5: precision on the free response.**
- Free-response points come from specific wording. Grade your answers strictly against the scoring guidelines, and learn what each task verb (identify, describe, explain, justify) requires.
- Don't neglect your strong units; small slips across many questions add up.

**Aiming for a 4: master the heavy units.**
- Use the unit weights in the Course and Exam Description. Make sure the highest-weight units are solid before polishing the rest.
- Do one free-response question per week from February on.

**Aiming for a solid 3: collect the reachable points.**
- Focus on multiple-choice accuracy in the big units and on the parts of free-response questions that ask you to identify or describe; they're the most accessible points.
- Short daily practice beats occasional long sessions.

sections.h2: Subject tips
sections.body:
| Subject | What it rewards | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| AP Biology | Experimental design, graphing and data analysis, not just content recall | [AP Biology exam format](/guide/ap-biology-exam-format) |
| AP Psychology | Applying concepts to scenarios and using research as evidence in the AAQ and EBQ | [AP Psychology exam format](/guide/ap-psychology-exam-format) |
| AP Environmental Science | Cause-and-effect chains, solutions and simple calculations with units | [APES exam format](/guide/ap-environmental-science-exam-format) |
| AP U.S. Government | Applying required cases and foundational documents to new situations | [Required Supreme Court cases](/guide/ap-us-government-required-supreme-court-cases) |

If you're self-studying, see [How to Self-Study AP Biology](/guide/how-to-self-study-ap-biology) for a week-by-week model you can adapt to other subjects.

sections.h2: Common mistakes
sections.body:
1. **Starting review in late April.** There isn't enough time to fix weak units and practice the format.
2. **Rereading instead of practicing.** Recognizing your notes isn't the same as answering a question about them.
3. **Skipping free-response practice.** Many students only practice multiple choice, then lose points to wording on the free response.
4. **Grading yourself generously.** Use the official scoring guidelines and be strict.
5. **Ignoring unit weights.** A weak unit worth 20% deserves far more time than one worth 6%.
6. **Cramming several exams the night before.** If you're taking multiple AP exams, plan your review around the earliest dates.

To see where a practice test puts you, try the free [AP score calculators](/ap-score-calculator) for APES, AP Biology, AP Psychology and AP U.S. Government.

faq.question: When should I start studying for AP exams?
faq.answer: Keep up with each unit during the year, then start dedicated review about two to three months before your exam, in February or March for May exams.

faq.question: What score do you need on an AP exam to get college credit?
faq.answer: It depends on the college and the subject. Many colleges grant credit or placement for a 3 or higher, and some require a 4 or 5. Check each college's AP credit policy.

faq.question: How do I get a 5 on an AP exam?
faq.answer: Master the highest-weight units, practice the free-response questions and grade them strictly against the official scoring guidelines, take timed practice exams and review every mistake.

faq.question: Can you self-study for an AP exam?
faq.answer: Yes. You'll need a school or authorized test center to order the exam for you, usually by mid-November, and a plan built around the Course and Exam Description and released exam questions.
